HEARD:

January 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23, 24, 25 and February 23, 2018

Akbarali J.:

Background

[
1
]

The parties, Ms. Marlene Bedzow-Weisleder (who now goes by Ms. Bedzow)
and Dr. Louis Weisleder, married on December 26, 1993. They separated 21 years
later on January 1, 2015. This trial deals with a number of issues arising out
of the breakdown of their marriage.

[
2
]

Before marriage, Ms. Bedzow was a speech pathologist working full-time
in Miami, Florida, her hometown. Dr. Weisleder was finishing his residency in
Toronto, his hometown, and had already committed to a fellowship in Toronto. As
a result, after marriage Ms. Bedzow relocated to Toronto and almost immediately
found full-time work as a speech pathologist.

[
3
]

Soon after, the parties bought a home and started a family. Eventually
three children were born: J.W. in 1996, L.W. in 1997, and Z.W. in 2000.

[
4
]

Once the children arrived, Ms. Bedzow’s working arrangements changed.
For much of their childhood, she worked part-time in her own speech pathology
practice which she ran out of the basement of the parties’ home, and later, out
of rented space in a medical practice. At the same time, Dr. Weisleder built up
a successful practice as an orthopaedic surgeon and as a medical/legal
consultant.

[
5
]

After separation, the parties continued to reside together in their home
until August 31, 2016 when Dr. Weisleder purchased Ms. Bedzow’s interest in the
home and she moved to rental accommodations.

[
6
]

Currently, J.W. is 21 and in his last semester of study at an American
university (“U.S.U.”). L.W. is 19 and in her second last year of study at the
same U.S.U. She has three semesters of study remaining. The youngest child,
Z.W. is 17 ½ years old and in his final term of grade 12 at a Jewish day
school. He has been accepted to the same U.S.U. where his siblings are
studying.

[
7
]

Z.W. is the only child currently living at home and the only remaining
minor child of the marriage. His relationship with Ms. Bedzow is currently
strained. As of the time evidence was led at trial, Z.W. had not seen his
mother since Dec. 21, 2017.

Issues

[
8
]

This trial raises a number of issues for determination. I set these out
below:

a.

What
parenting arrangements should be in place for Z.W., the minor child of the
marriage?

b.

Should
a permanent order issue restraining the manner of Ms. Bedzow’s communications
with Dr. Weisleder, Z.W. and Dr. Weisleder’s new partner, B.H.?

c.

What
is required to equalize the value of net family property? This requires
determining how certain items must be treated for purposes of the equalization
calculation:

i.

Two joint TD (US) accounts;

ii.

Dr. Weisleder’s interest in Brace Yourself Orthotics Inc.;

iii.

Tax penalties and interest paid by Dr. Weisleder during the marriage and
refunded after separation;

iv.

A debt recorded on the books of 1286972 Ontario Ltd. (“128”) as owing by
Dr. Weisleder to 128. 128 is a corporation of which Dr. Weisleder is the sole
officer and director but which is owned by a trust, the beneficiaries of which
are the Weisleder children;

v.

Money borrowed from the bar and bat mitzvah accounts of two of the
children;

vi.

Ms. Bedzow’s engagement ring; and

vii.

Dr. Weisleder’s Rolex watch.

d.

Should
the contents of the matrimonial home be sold and the proceeds divided?

e.

What
prospective and retrospective orders should be made regarding child and spousal
support? Determining this requires considering the following issues:

i.

What is Dr. Weisleder’s income and means for support purposes for 2016,
2017 and prospectively?

ii.

What is Ms. Bedzow’s income and means for support purposes for 2016,
2017 and prospectively? Specifically, should income be imputed to her on the
basis that she can work more than she has been working?

iii.

What table support, if any, is owing for Z.W.?

iv.

How and in what proportion should the children’s s. 7 expenses be
funded? This requires considering the respective income and means of the
parties, the means available to the children, the assets held by 128, and
whether it is a reasonable and necessary expense for Z.W. to attend U.S.U.; and

v.

The parties agree that spousal support is payable. What is the
appropriate amount of spousal support and are any retroactive adjustments
warranted with respect to the support paid since separation?

f.

How should reimbursement of expenses Ms. Bedzow incurred that are
covered by Dr. Weisleder’s medical and dental benefits plan be dealt with?

[
9
]

I consider each of these issues below.

Analysis

Parenting

[
10
]

At the time of separation, Ms. Bedzow had a strained relationship with
J.W., her eldest child, and a good relationship with L.W. and Z.W., her younger
children. Since that time her relationships with all the children have
deteriorated.

[
11
]

Ms. Bedzow admitted to the difficulties in her relationships with the
children and expressed her belief that, once the trial was completed and the
financial issues settled, she could work on rebuilding them. She pointed out
that for many years, she and the children were close.

[
12
]

At the moment, her relationship with the children is fractured. Much of
this is as a result of the difficulties Ms. Bedzow has had in regulating her
emotional responses to the stress she is under.

[
13
]

There was significant evidence before me of Ms. Bedzow’s emails and text
messages, principally to Dr. Weisleder, but also to the children. In addition,
there was significant evidence before me of Ms. Bedzow’s Instagram posts. The
emails, texts and Instagram posts entered into evidence were harassing,
abusive, vulgar, and hateful. Many of these were sent in the latter part of
2017 when the conflict in this litigation was exceedingly high.

[
14
]

On October 19, 2017, Kristjanson J. issued a temporary order pursuant to

s. 28
(c)
(1)
and
(2)
of the
Children’s Law Reform Act,
R.S.O. 1990, c. C.12
[“
CLRA
”], restraining Ms. Bedzow from sending Dr. Weisleder any text
messages or emails unless they are necessary to communicate important
information about the children, and in such cases, directing that the emails be
polite and courteous and contain no emojis.

[
15
]

Of her own motion, Kristjanson J. directed Ms. Bedzow not to communicate
with Z.W. in an abusive, emotionally threatening and inappropriate manner, and
directed that communications with Z.W. had to be polite and courteous.

[
16
]

Kristjanson J.’s order also set out a temporary parenting schedule,
under which Z.W. is supposed to spend about half his time with each parent.

[
17
]

Ms. Bedzow admits that she has breached Kristjanson J.’s order with
respect to her communications with both Dr. Weisleder and Z.W.

[
18
]

I address Dr. Weisleder’s request for a permanent restraining order in
my analysis of that issue. Here, I relate this history to point out that,
despite Kristjanson J.’s clear reasons highlighting the negative emotional
impact that these communications have on Z.W., Ms. Bedzow has continued to
engage in these destructive communications.

[
19
]

For example, in December 2017 Ms. Bedzow texted Z.W. to tell him that
she would sit shiva for him, in effect telling him that he was dead to her. It
is clear this text was a breach of Kristjanson J.’s order, in that it was
abusive, emotionally threatening and inappropriate. The evidence at trial was
that, despite the temporary parenting schedule Kristjanson J. ordered in
October 2017, Z.W. had not seen Ms. Bedzow since she sent that text. However,
when the parties reattended for closing arguments, they filed an agreed
statement of facts which indicated that Z.W. is once again spending time with
Ms. Bedzow, in a manner that suggests the temporary parenting schedule
Kristjanson J. ordered is once again being followed, more or less.

[
20
]

The agreed statement of facts filed during closing argument also
indicates that Ms. Bedzow continues to engage in harassing conduct towards Dr.
Weisleder. It also includes a text from Z.W. suggesting that Ms. Bedzow
continues to communicate abusively towards him, and that he blames both his
parents for putting him in the middle of their dispute. This text is hearsay,
but is admitted for proof of the fact that Z.W. made those statements.

[
21
]

In considering the appropriate parenting order,
s. 16
of the
Divorce Act
,
R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2
nd
Supp.) provides that the sole criterion for
determining custody and access is Z.W.’s best interests, as determined by
reference to his condition, means, needs and other circumstances. In considering
the best interests of the child, the criteria set out in
ss. 20
and
24
of the
CLRA

are relevant, and include the love, affection and emotional ties between the
child and each parent, the child’s views and preferences, and the ability of
each person applying for custody or access to act as a parent:
Marrello v.
Marrello
,
2016 ONSC 835
, at paras.
108 and 110
.

[
22
]

Z.W. is nearly an adult. He will turn 18 in May 2018. Given his age, I
must place considerable weight on his wishes:
Kaplanis v. Kaplanis
(2005),

2005 CanLII 1625 (ON CA)
, 249 D.L.R. (4
th
) 620 (C.A.), at paras.
10 and 13
;
Kincl v.
Malkova,
2008 ONCA 524
, at para.
3
. Z.W. did not testify at trial, but Dr.
Weisleder testified as to Z.W.’s emotional upset at the text he received from
Ms. Bedzow. Dr. Weisleder’s evidence was that Z.W. prefers to spend his time
with Dr. Weisleder at his home rather than with Ms. Bedzow at her home.

[
23
]

Ms. Bedzow testified as to her belief that Dr. Weisleder has been
disparaging her to the children. Other than her belief, there is no evidence of
this disparagement. Dr. Weisleder did admit that he would not encourage Z.W. to
respect the temporary parenting schedule put in place in the October 2017 order
of Kristjanson J. He explained that he had previously encouraged all the
children to spend time with Ms. Bedzow, but that after the text Ms. Bedzow sent
to Z.W. telling him she would sit shiva for him, he would not encourage Z.W. to
spend time with Ms. Bedzow. However, since visits between Z.W. and Ms. Bedzow
have resumed, it appears that Dr. Weisleder is, at least, not impeding Z.W.’s
ability to spend time with Ms. Bedzow.

[
24
]

As I understand Dr. Weisleder’s evidence, he is responding to what he
views as the emotional damage Ms. Bedzow has done to Z.W., and is expressing an
unwillingness to encourage Z.W. to put himself in a position to be further
damaged by Ms. Bedzow’s inability to regulate her emotions. I share these
concerns. I am not convinced that in her current emotional state, Ms. Bedzow
has the ability to regulate her emotions or the ability to consistently parent
Z.W. without behaving in an emotionally abusive manner.

[
25
]

In my view, it is in Z.W.’s best interests to set aside the parenting
schedule ordered by Kristjanson J. and not replace it. At nearly 18 years old,
and having been caught in the crossfire of this high conflict dispute between
his parents, I find that it is in Z.W.’s best interests to decide for himself where
he spends his time.

[
26
]

The parties also sought, on consent, an order addressing how they should
share holidays with all the children, including J.W. and L.W. who are now
adults. I have no jurisdiction to direct adult children where to spend their
holidays. The parties are free to communicate to their children the agreement
that they have reached, but it is up to the children individually to decide how
and where they will spend their time.

Restraining Order

[
27
]

Dr. Weisleder seeks to make the restraining order issued by Kristjanson
J. permanent and seeks to expand it to include a restriction on Ms. Bedzow
directing communication to his current partner, B.H., on Instagram for a period
of one year.

[
28
]

I have already noted above the ample evidence of abusive communications
that caused Kristjanson J. to issue the order she did. Since the order was
issued, Ms. Bedzow has violated it through further communications, including
after the evidentiary phase of the trial, although overall there appear to be
fewer instances of abusive communication than before Kristjanson J.’s order was
issued. The order appears to have had some ameliorating effect on Ms. Bedzow’s
conduct.

[
29
]

In addition to the texts and emails that were before Kristjanson J. and
those entered into evidence at trial, the evidence before me included posts Ms.
Bedzow made on her Instagram account directed at Dr. Weisleder and his current
partner. Ms. Bedzow has over 200 followers on Instagram, some of whom are known
to both Ms. Bedzow and Dr. Weisleder and are part of their common community.
Until very recently when she blocked them, the children followed Ms. Bedzow on
Instagram. Ms. Bedzow deposed that her posts were designed to make B.H. aware
of Dr. Weisleder’s true character. Ms. Bedzow acknowledged that her followers
could infer that the posts were directed at Dr. Weisleder. Dr. Weisleder
testified that seeing those posts embarrassed and shamed the children.

[
30
]

During this two week trial, after being cross-examined on a number of
her Instagram posts, Ms. Bedzow continued to post objectionable content on
Instagram. For example, after Ms. Bedzow called B.H. to testify (under summons)
she posted about “#botoxBarbieface” and “#vapidcouples”. She posted about the
trial using the hashtag “weekwon onto weaktwo”. Ms. Bedzow does not seem to be
able to help herself.

[
31
]

Ms. Bedzow argues that no continuing restraining order is necessary, because
once the trial is resolved, the conflict will be concluded and the height of
the turmoil will have passed. The fact that Ms. Bedzow’s conduct continued, in
spite of Kristjanson J.’s order and during the trial itself gives me no
confidence that Ms. Bedzow’s assertion is correct. The recency of her conduct,
both during and after the evidentiary phase of the trial, suggests that she
will continue to engage in harassing and abusive communications through text,
email and Instagram if her conduct is not regulated by order.

[
32
]

The question is therefore not whether the evidence justifies the order,
but whether I have the jurisdiction to grant it. I have made no order as to
custody or access, so
s. 28
of the
CLRA

under which Kristjanson J.
issued the temporary restraining order has no application.

[
33
]

Dr. Weisleder relies on
s. 46(1)
of the
Family Law Act
, R.S.O.
1990, c. F.3 [“
FLA
”] which provides that a court may make a final
restraining order against a former spouse if the applicant has reasonable
grounds to fear for his own safety or for the safety of any child in his lawful
custody.

[
34
]

The relevant factors for granting such an order are set out in
Tiveron
v. Collins
,
2014 ONCJ 517
, at paras.
168-169
[“
Tiveron
”]: (i) the
applicant must have a reasonable fear for his safety; (ii) the fear may be
entirely subjective as long as it is legitimate; and (iii) the fear may be
equally for psychological safety as well as for physical safety.

[
35
]

I conclude that Ms. Bedzow’s communications engender a legitimate fear in
Dr. Weisleder for his psychological safety. In evidence, Dr. Weisleder
confirmed the highly upsetting nature of Ms. Bedzow’s communications. The
communications are emotionally abusive and Dr. Weisleder should not be subject
to them. I thus conclude that the grounds for a permanent restraining order with
respect to Ms. Bedzow’s communications to Dr. Weisleder under
s. 46(1)
of the
FLA

have been made out.

[
36
]

With respect to Z.W., I note that
s. 46(1)
refers to the safety of any
child in the “lawful custody” of the applicant, and I have made no order as to
custody. In closing arguments, I asked the parties if I would have jurisdiction
to make a restraining order with respect to communications with Z.W. under this
section if I made no custody order. Ms. Bedzow indicated that she would not
make a strong argument against my jurisdiction. Dr. Weisleder argued that in
any event I have broad
parens patriae
jurisdiction to make any order
that is in the best interests of a child.

[
37
]

In my view, a restraining order should issue with respect to Ms.
Bedzow’s communications with Z.W., and I have jurisdiction to issue it based on
my
parens patriae
jurisdiction. The order will thus be effective until
he turns 18 years old.

[
38
]

Ms. Bedzow raised some concern with respect to the specificity of the
order, and the difficulty in fashioning a clear order. In my view, the order of
Kristjanson J. is clear. Ms. Bedzow has breached it, and has admitted breaching
it. She understands what it requires of her, and she understands she has fallen
short. I therefore conclude that Kristjanson J.’s order shall be permanently
continued with respect to Dr. Weisleder, and continued with respect to Z.W.
while he remains a minor.

[
39
]

The issue of the restraining order is more complicated with respect to
B.H. Dr. Weisleder relies on
Callon v. Callon
,
1999 CanLII 35002 (ON SCDC)
, 1999 CarswellOnt 2401 (Ont.
Div. Ct.), at para.
1
for the proposition that an order can be made respecting
communications by a former spouse to a third party under
s. 46(1)

FLA
.

[
40
]

I accept that
s. 46(1)

FLA

can be used in that manner. However,
the criteria in
Tiveron
remain applicable. B.H. testified at trial but
gave no evidence as to any fear for her psychological safety caused by the
Instagram posts. The
Tiveron
criteria are not made out on the evidence
with respect to B.H.

[
41
]

Therefore, Dr. Weisleder’s request for a restraining order with respect
to Ms. Bedzow’s communications towards him and Z.W. is granted. I decline to
order a restraining order with respect to Ms. Bedzow’s communications directed
at B.H.

[
42
]

Although there is no basis for an order with respect to B.H., I urge Ms.
Bedzow to stop directing Instagram posts at B.H. If Ms. Bedzow wishes to
rebuild her relationship with her children, as she states she does, her
emotional self-regulation will need to improve and she will need to move on
with her life. Instagram posts directed at B.H. will work against this goal.

Equalizing the Value of Net Family Property

[
43
]

The value of the parties’ net family property must be equalized as of
the valuation day. In this case, the parties agree valuation day is January 1,
2015, the date on which they separated with no reasonable prospect that they
would resume cohabitation. The parties disagree about the treatment of certain
items in dispute.

[
44
]

I note that the parties agree that Ms. Bedzow’s credit card debt that
existed at separation was paid by Dr. Weisleder and is properly considered his
debt at separation in the NFP calculation.

[
45
]

Below I will consider the items about which the parties disagree.

The TD (US) Accounts

[
46
]

Ms. Bedzow’s father died while the parties were married. Although he
died without a will, Ms. Bedzow’s mother decided to give each member of the
family $25,000 USD as an inheritance from Ms. Bedzow’s father. Thus, Ms.
Bedzow, Dr. Weisleder and the children each received $25,000 USD. The total
amount was placed into two TD (US) accounts, held jointly by Dr. Weisleder and
Ms. Bedzow. One of the accounts held $122,500 USD; the other held $2,500 USD.
These facts are not in dispute.

[
47
]

After separation, Ms. Bedzow removed the funds from the joint accounts.
She has given each of the children 1/5 of the amount she took from the account
that held $122,500, consisting of their 1/5 share in the capital and interest
thereon, but she has not returned Dr. Weisleder’s 1/5 share to him. She has not
distributed to anyone their share of the funds in the $2,500 account including
its growth.

[
48
]

Ms. Bedzow and Dr. Weisleder agree that 1/5 of the funds that were in
the $122,500 account belong to Dr. Weisleder, consisting of his 1/5 share of
the capital and his 1/5 share of the growth.

[
49
]

There originally appeared to be disagreement with respect to the account
that held $2,500, an amount that has increased due to the accrued interest. At
closing arguments it became clear that the parties agree that the funds in this
account should be split five ways with each of Ms. Bedzow, Dr. Weisleder and
the children getting a 1/5 share.

[
50
]

The parties agree that this inheritance from Ms. Bedzow’s father should
be isolated from the net family property calculation. In my view this is appropriate.
I direct Ms. Bedzow to pay Dr. Weisleder his 1/5 share from both accounts, and
to pay the children their 1/5 share from the $2,500 account.

Brace Yourself Orthotics Inc.

[
51
]

Dr. Weisleder owns 28 shares, amounting to a 23.3% interest, in a
company called Brace Yourself Orthotics Inc. Brace Yourself Orthotics’
financial year end is February 28, 2018.

[
52
]

Dr. Weisleder testified that he usually receives a dividend cheque from
Brace Yourself Orthotics once or twice a year. He is not in control of when
dividends get declared or in what amount.

[
53
]

Ms. Bedzow argues that, as of valuation day, Dr. Weisleder was owed
money from Brace Yourself Orthotics. She relies on the February 28, 2015 year-end
financial statements which reflect “bonus payable” and “due to shareholder”
amounts of $11,937 and $47,748 respectively. She argues that Dr. Weisleder’s
share of these amounts is $13,727.55 and should be reflected as an amount owed
to him in the NFP calculation. The productions include a cheque to Dr. Weisleder
from Brace Yourself Orthotics in the amount of $11,481 dated August 7, 2015
with the notation “YE 2015”.

[
54
]

There is no evidence before me as to the value of the shares of Brace
Yourself Orthotics. In any event, Ms. Bedzow makes no claim for equalization of
value of the shares as a capital asset. The only evidence is about the dividend
income that Dr. Weisleder received. This amount has been included in his income
calculation for support purposes.

[
55
]

In my view, the dividend income from Brace Yourself Orthotics would be
double counted if it were both, in Dr. Weisleder’s income for support purposes
and on his NFP statement as a receivable. Moreover, I note that in 2015, the
parties continued their financial status quo for almost the entire year. They
continued to reside in the matrimonial home together and financed their lives
as they always had, until November 2015 when Dr. Weisleder restricted Ms.
Bedzow’s use of the parties’ joint credit card. The dividends from Brace
Yourself Orthotics thus benefitted both parties in 2015 as income available to
them.

[
56
]

Accordingly, I conclude that the dividend income Dr. Weisleder received
should be considered as part of his income for support purposes and not as an
asset on his NFP statement.

Tax Interest and Penalties Paid Before Separation and
Refunded After Separation

[
57
]

Dr. Weisleder and Ms. Bedzow did not file tax returns for the years
2007-2010. Eventually those returns were prepared and filed together with the
2011 returns, which were filed on time in the spring of 2012. The late tax returns
were thus finally filed about three years before valuation day.

[
58
]

Because of the late filing of the 2007-2010 returns, CRA charged penalties
and interest of $155,895.85 to Dr. Weisleder. He paid the taxes owing,
penalties and interest before separation, in two payments made in May and
August 2012.

[
59
]

Also before separation, in 2014, Dr. Weisleder asked CRA to waive the
penalties and interest arising from the late filing. (In effect, he sought a
refund since he had already paid the penalties and interest.) In support of his
request, he disclosed certain health-related stresses he faced at the time he
failed to file his returns, and which continued. His request was refused in
correspondence from the CRA dated January 22, 2015, three weeks after separation.
Dr. Weisleder then wrote to CRA again in October 2015 to provide further
information and ask that his request be reconsidered. Dr. Weisleder did not
explain why he waited ten months to respond to CRA’s letter. Fourteen months
after separation, CRA forgave the penalties and interest and refunded the
entire $155,895.85 to Dr. Weisleder.

[
60
]

Dr. Weisleder agrees that this amount should be reflected on his NFP
statement, but argues it should be discounted by half because it was contingent
at the time of separation. He states it was highly unlikely that he would
receive any refund at all.

[
61
]

Ms. Bedzow argues that the family’s financial circumstances were
burdened by the penalties and interest. She argues that the entirety of the
refund should be included in Dr. Weisleder’s NFP statement.

[
62
]

The unfiled tax returns were a problem for the family. Neither party
filed their tax returns. Although Ms. Bedzow devoted much energy at trial to
blaming Dr. Weisleder for the failure to file the returns, I do not accept that
she was unaware of the problem. She claims not to have known about the unfiled
returns until sometime after her father’s death in December 2011. She also
admits that in the years prior to 2008 (when the 2007 returns should have been
prepared) she would provide information to the parties’ accountant, and would
review her tax returns. I do not accept that she was not aware that the tax
returns for 2007-2010 were not filed. As an adult who had filed tax returns
before, she knew that she had not filed her returns for those years.

[
63
]

The failure to file the tax returns was driven in part by the lack of
money to pay the taxes, as the money that should have been allocated for taxes
was used to fund family expenses. As will become apparent later in these
reasons, in my view this family lived beyond their means for many years,
enjoying a lifestyle funded in no small part by debt. In 2008-2011, the debt
included the taxes owed to CRA which were unpaid. The manner of funding their
lifestyle has infected all aspects of the parties’ finances and they must bear
equal responsibility for those decisions. Similarly, to the extent that there
was amelioration of their financial circumstances, both parties should equally
benefit.

[
64
]

Dr. Weisleder began the process of applying for the refund before
separation. The refund would have come very shortly after separation had he not
waited ten months to respond to CRA’s letter of January 24 2015. Even still,
the refund was received only fourteen months after separation and relates to
funds paid out to CRA during the marriage.

[
65
]

I conclude that to avoid a windfall to Dr. Weisleder, the full amount of
the CRA refund should be included in his NFP statement.

Debt to 1286972 Ontario Ltd.

[
66
]

The most contentious item between the parties relates to Dr. Weisleder’s
claimed debt to 128. 128 is a corporation of which Dr. Weisleder is the sole
officer and director. The corporation is wholly owned by the Weisleder Family
Trust. The sole beneficiaries of the trust are J.W., L.W., and Z.W.

[
67
]

The trust documents show that the settlor and a trustee of the trust is
Mark Weisleder, Dr. Weisleder’s brother. They show Dr. Weisleder as a trustee.
Ms. Bedzow is also shown as a trustee, but unlike Dr. and Mr. Weisleder, she
does not appear to have signed the trust documentation. Without trust
documentation signed by Ms. Bedzow, I accept her argument that she has never
been a trustee of the trust.

[
68
]

Mr. Weisleder’s evidence, which I accept, is that he signed the trust
documents but has had nothing to do with the trust since that time,
notwithstanding his designation as trustee. It appears that the decisions
regarding the trust have been made by Dr. Weisleder.

[
69
]

Since the creation of 128 until the beginning of 2016, Dr. Weisleder
directed all of his non-OHIP income into 128’s account. Dr. Weisleder states
that the purpose of doing so was to build up money for the children to assist
them in establishing themselves in their adult lives. Dr. Weisleder explained that
both he and Ms. Bedzow are children of Holocaust survivors, and that it was
important to their parents to assist Dr. Weisleder and Ms. Bedzow in
establishing themselves by helping them buy a house. He states that he and Ms.
Bedzow wished to do the same for their children.

[
70
]

Saving to help the children get a good start to their adult lives may
have been a motivation behind establishing the corporation, but the corporate
structure was common for doctors to employ because of the tax benefits it
offered. The corporate tax rate was lower than Dr. Weisleder’s marginal rate and
savings could be generated by retaining earnings in the corporation. With the
structure of the family trust and 128, Dr. Weisleder was in a position to
dividend out income to the trust, and through it to the children, at a lower
marginal tax rate than he would pay if he treated his non-OHIP income as his
income for tax purposes.

[
71
]

Over the years, however, Dr. Weisleder withdrew significant amounts from
128 to pay family expenses. These are booked as “loans to shareholder” although
Dr. Weisleder is not a shareholder of 128. Because he was not a shareholder,
his understanding is that he could withdraw the funds from 128 as a loan and
repay it later without having to pay income tax. His accountant confirmed that
this was the structure they employed. Dr. Weisleder said that without the money
from 128, the family could not have met its expenses.

[
72
]

I note that there were also loans by Dr. Weisleder to 128, particularly
with respect to a family cottage that was purchased through 128. I address the
assets held by 128, including the proceeds from the sale of that cottage, when
I consider the issues around support, below.

[
73
]

For the purposes of equalization, it is only relevant to understand that
Dr. Weisleder claims to owe 128 $824,297 in respect of the loans he took from
the corporation. His accountant states that the figure may be as high as
$910,000 but $824,297 is the amount disclosed on 128’s 2014 financial
statements. In my view, the financial statements are the best evidence of the
amount. Dr. Weisleder claims this amount on his NFP statement as a debt owing
at valuation day.

[
74
]

Ms. Bedzow disputes this debt. She argues that Dr. Weisleder controls
128 and it is his alter ego. She argues that any debt owing to 128 is a debt
Dr. Weisleder owes to himself and is thus of no consequence to equalization.

[
75
]

Ms. Bedzow relies on
Locke v. Locke
,
2000 BCSC 1300
, at para.
23

[“
Locke
”], where the court set out seven factors to consider to
determine if monies advanced truly constitute a loan. These are: (i) whether
there were any contemporaneous documents evidencing a loan; (ii) whether the
manner for repayment is specified; (iii) whether there is security held for the
loan; (iv) whether there are advances to one child and not others, or advances
of unequal amounts to various children; (v) whether there has been any demand
for payment before the separation of the parties; (vi) whether there has been
any partial repayment; and (vii) whether there was any expectation or
likelihood of repayment.

[
76
]

Ms. Bedzow correctly notes that the case law on
bona fide
loans
focuses on advances of money from parents to children where the children are
adults involved in family litigation. It is thus not on all fours with this
situation. However, Ms. Bedzow argues that the principles are applicable to
loans from a corporation to its sole operator and alter ego. She argues that
the debt to 128 does not satisfy the
Locke

test and is not
bona fide
.

[
77
]

Counsel could not point me to any case law that applies the
Locke

factors
in the context of loans to a party from a company controlled by that party.

[
78
]

In my view, the
Locke

factors are of limited utility in
evaluating whether the loan from 128 to Dr. Weisleder is
bona fide.
The
factors that look at whether the manner of repayment is specified, whether
security is held for the debt and whether there have been any demands for
repayment are not helpful indicators when the alleged debtor is also the sole
officer and director of the corporation. The factor that looks at unequal
advances to various children does not apply.

[
79
]

The only factors that assist in evaluating the legitimacy of Dr.
Weisleder’s claimed debt to 128 are whether the loan was documented
contemporaneously, whether it has been partially repaid and whether it is
expected to be or likely to be repaid. With respect to these factors, I note:

a.

the
loan is documented on 128’s financial statements throughout;

b.

Dr.
Weisleder testified that he has partially repaid the loan by paying some of
128’s tax liabilities from his funds; and

c.

Dr.
Weisleder’s evidence is that he expects to repay the debt when he is able, when
the children have completed their studies. However, he has no real plan for how
to repay the loan. As a last resort he testified that the proceeds from a life
insurance policy held by 128 against his life could be used to repay the loan
on his death. I note this evidence is confusing, as the life insurance (which I
address further below) is either an asset of 128 or is security for the loan. In
closing argument, Dr. Weisleder’s counsel acknowledged that the life insurance
policy could not be considered security for the loan.

[
80
]

In addition to these factors, I have also considered the third party
interests at stake. The funds that came into 128 were generated by Dr.
Weisleder’s non-OHIP work, but once those funds were placed into 128, they
became beneficially owned by the children, who are the sole beneficiaries of
the trust which is the sole shareholder of 128. Setting up this structure may
have been a wise decision for tax planning or for saving for the children, but
it was not a wise decision if the parties needed Dr. Weisleder’s non-OHIP
income to fund the ongoing expenses of their family. Nevertheless, it was the
decision they made. The money in 128 belonged beneficially to the children. It
was not a tax-free piggy bank from which the parties could take money without
consequence.

[
81
]

Ms. Bedzow argues she did not know that Dr. Weisleder was borrowing from
128, while Dr. Weisleder states that they talked about their finances and he
pleaded with Ms. Bedzow to reduce her spending. I prefer Dr. Weisleder’s
evidence on this point. Ms. Bedzow’s entire approach to the family’s spending
seemed to be that it was Dr. Weisleder’s responsibility to provide a certain
lifestyle for her and the family, and any failure to do so should be borne
entirely by him. I reject this contention. Neither party should be insulated
from the consequences of their financial decisions.

[
82
]

Accordingly, I conclude the debt is
bona fide
and should be a
valuation day deduction from Dr. Weisleder’s NFP.

[
83
]

Given my conclusion, it is not necessary to address Ms. Bedzow’s
alternative argument that, if the money is not a debt and instead is considered
income to Dr. Weisleder he has failed to prove the tax liability that arises
out of that income such that no tax liability should be allocated to him.
However, had I found the debt was not
bona fide
and the funds were
actually income that Dr. Weisleder took without paying tax on it, I would have assessed
his tax liability at 46%, the marginal rate at which Dr. Weisleder calculated
his income tax obligation. It would defy common sense to think that the funds
could be considered income without a resulting tax liability. Indeed, in these
circumstances, if the funds were income rather than debt, Dr. Weisleder would
also be facing significant interest and penalties from CRA from his failure to
pay tax on the income.

Money Borrowed from J.W. and L.W.’s Bar and Bat
Mitzvah Accounts

[
84
]

The parties disagree about how to treat money borrowed from J.W. and
L.W.’s bar and bat mitzvah accounts.

[
85
]

Because J.W. and L.W. are close in age, the parties were able to arrange
a b’nai mitzvah for them both. The party they held was elaborate and costly.
The expenses for the b’nai mitzvah were over $150,000.

[
86
]

J.W. and L.W. each received approximately $18,000 in money gifts from
the b’nai mitzvah. These amounts were deposited into accounts for each of them.

[
87
]

Ms. Bedzow testified that the parties decided to use the funds to pay
for a trip to Israel to attend the bar mitzvah of J.W.’s close friend. Dr.
Weisleder testified that the money was withdrawn to pay for family expenses,
but he denies the expenses were for the trip to Israel. The bank statements
show that amounts were taken out piecemeal rather than in one large withdrawal.

[
88
]

In my view, it does not matter whether the money was used for the trip
or to meet other family expenses. There was only one pot of money. The problem
was that it was too small for the way the parties lived.

[
89
]

Ms. Bedzow argues that, at most, Dr. Weisleder has a moral obligation to
pay the money back, but no legal obligation so it should not form a deduction
from his NFP as a debt owing on separation. Dr. Weisleder argues that this is a
debt he must pay back.

[
90
]

In her evidence at trial, Ms. Bedzow stated that she expected Dr.
Weisleder to repay J.W. and L.W. the money he took from their accounts. I note
that despite the fact that the money was used either for family expenses or for
the family trip, Ms. Bedzow expressed no personal responsibility to pay back
the money; rather that is an obligation she thinks belongs to Dr. Weisleder and
in which she need not share.

[
91
]

Ms. Bedzow also argues that the money taken from the bar and bat mitzvah
accounts does not meet the
Locke
criteria and is not a
bona fide
loan.

[
92
]

In my view, the
Locke
criteria do not have ready application when
the lender is a minor child of the borrower, as J.W. and L.W. were at the time
their b’nai mitzvah money was used for the family. One would not expect a
twelve or thirteen year old to demand security. Nor would I expect a child of
the borrower to demand repayment, especially during a time in their lives when
(as here) they continue to depend on the borrower for financial support to
finish their education.

[
93
]

In view of Ms. Bedzow’s evidence that she expects Dr. Weisleder to pay
the children back, I am satisfied that when the money was withdrawn, both Ms.
Bedzow and Dr. Weisleder expected the borrowing to be temporary and the money
to be returned to J.W. and L.W. I thus conclude that the debt is a
bona fide

debt which serves as a deduction from Dr. Weisleder’s NFP.

Value of Ms. Bedzow’s Engagement Ring

[
94
]

Ms. Bedzow estimates the value of her engagement ring at the time of
marriage to be $25,000. Dr. Weisleder estimates its value to be $10,000.

[
95
]

In their fifteenth year of marriage, to commemorate their tenth wedding
anniversary, the parties upgraded the ring although they could ill-afford to do
so. Ms. Bedzow states that the appraised value of the ring is $38,000. She
argues that more than half of the value of the ring was founded on its original
valuation day value, such that less of the appraised value at separation should
be equalized.

[
96
]

Dr. Weisleder testified that when they upgraded the ring, they exchanged
the original two carat stone for a bigger five carat stone, and that to pay for
the difference, he withdrew $50,000 from the parties’ line of credit.

[
97
]

It is not clear where Ms. Bedzow gets her estimate of $25,000 for the
original ring. I do not accept this estimate. First, Dr. Weisleder is the one
who purchased the ring. He is more likely to know what it cost. Second, if the
upgrade cost $50,000 plus the exchange of the original two carat stone, I do
not accept that the ring’s value increased by only $13,000. I saw no evidence
documenting the purchase price or the price paid to upgrade the ring.

[
98
]

I conclude that Dr. Weisleder’s original estimate of the ring’s value is
correct. I base this conclusion on the fact that he is the one that bought it,
and on the fact that the appraised value of the ring after upgrading must
account for a significant increase in value of the ring given what Dr.
Weisleder paid to upgrade it. I thus find that the ring was worth $10,000 on
marriage and $38,000 on separation.

Dr. Weisleder’s Rolex Watch

[
99
]

Dr. Weisleder owns a Rolex watch that he testified was a gift from his
parents and as such is excluded property:
Hamilton v. Hamilton
(1996),

1996 CanLII 599 (ON CA)
, 92 O.A.C. 103 (C.A.), at para.
49
. Ms. Bedzow argues that the value of Dr.
Weisleder’s watch should not be excluded from his NFP. She states that the
watch was a symbolic gift that Dr. Weisleder purchased for himself but that was
notionally from his parents. Ms. Bedzow states that the watch was paid for out
of the family’s finances. She states that Dr. Weisleder purchased this symbolic
gift as a gesture to his mother when she was terminally ill. Ms. Bedzow argues
that Dr. Weisleder’s parents were of modest means and they had just helped the
couple buy their first house the year before. She states they would not have
had the money to buy him the watch.

[
100
]

Other
than her statement as to belief, Ms. Bedzow has no other evidence to back up
this claim. She does not know where the money came from to buy the watch. She
notes that Dr. Weisleder did not ask his brother about the origin of the watch
when his brother testified, and argues that I should draw an adverse inference
from that fact. I decline to do so. Ms. Bedzow is the party who called Mr.
Weisleder and she did not ask him either.

[
101
]

Ms.
Bedzow also argues that the watch is worth more than the $10,000 Dr. Weisleder
claims it is worth, but that he never got it appraised to determine its value.

[
102
]

Dr.
Weisleder testified that upon completing his fellowship, his parents wanted to
buy him a gold watch. He refused this gift until 1996 because he felt the gift
was too expensive for his parents given their means. However, he states that he
eventually accepted the gift. He stated that he paid nothing for the watch.

[
103
]

I
prefer Dr. Weisleder’s evidence on this point. His parents may have been of
limited means, but I accept that they wished to mark the completion of his
fellowship with a meaningful gift, in the same way that they provided funds to
Dr. Weisleder and Ms. Bedzow to buy a house. I accept that it was important to
them to sacrifice for their children. This is a lesson Dr. Weisleder has taken
on and applies to his own children. It was clear to me that in doing so, he is
trying to honour the example his parents set for him.

[
104
]

Moreover,
I do not accept that Dr. Weisleder buying his own watch would have been any
kind of gesture to his ill mother. The watch would have had meaning to Dr.
Weisleder’s parents if it were their gift to him, not him spending his money on
himself.

[
105
]

Accordingly,
I conclude that the value of the watch is excluded property. There is thus no
reason to consider whether it has been undervalued. The watch shall be shown
and excluded at $10,000 on Dr. Weisleder’s NFP statement.

Conclusion on Equalization

[
106
]

In
view of the determinations I have made above, I have calculated that Ms. Bedzow
owes Dr. Weisleder an equalization payment of $451,385.99. The calculation is
attached at Schedule A. It does not include the items disclosed on the parties’
NFP statements which the parties agree have no or nominal value.

[
107
]

However,
the amount of the equalization payment is not the only issue.

[
108
]

The
effect of the conclusions I have reached is that Ms. Bedzow will owe a
significant equalization payment to Dr. Weisleder, in large part because I have
found the debt to 128 is
bona fide
. But in his evidence, Dr. Weisleder
testified that he was not sure when he would be able to repay the debt (beyond
the small repayment he has made to date). He suggested he would seek to begin
repaying it once the children are all finished their university studies.

[
109
]

Since
Dr. Weisleder has control over when he will repay the debt, there is potential
hardship, in that Ms. Bedzow would have to deplete a large portion of her
savings to make the equalization payment which Dr. Weisleder may or may not
choose to use to repay the debt to 128 (or, roughly, Ms. Bedzow’s effective
responsibility for half of it) and he may choose not to repay his half of the
debt at the same time.

[
110
]

Some
of this inequity is dealt with, below, in my assessment of how the assets of
128, including the debt Dr. Weisleder owes it, should be considered in the
context of the children’s s. 7 expenses. But I also conclude that it is
appropriate to order the equalization payment to be made over a ten year period
to avoid hardship to Ms. Bedzow:
FLA
, s. 9(1)(c)
.
I thus conclude
that Ms. Bedzow shall pay the equalization payment to Dr. Weisleder in ten
equal installments, beginning thirty days after the judgment is signed, with the
next nine payments to be made annually on the anniversary date of the judgment.

[
111
]

My
determination that the equalization payment should be paid over ten years
raises the question of whether interest should accrue on the amount owing. I
will require submissions on this issue, and provide directions with respect to
those submissions in para. 225 below.

Contents of the Matrimonial Home

[
112
]

The
parties disagree about the treatment of the contents of the matrimonial home.

[
113
]

The
parties negotiated the price at which Dr. Weisleder would purchase Ms. Bedzow’s
interest in the matrimonial home. Dr. Weisleder testified that originally they

114
]

After
Ms. Bedzow sold her interest in the home to Dr. Weisleder, she moved into

[
115
]

Ms.
Bedzow continued to seek additional contents. Efforts at dividing the contents

116
]

Mr.
Greber was qualified as an expert in these proceedings (without objection from

]

Ms.

accept Mr. Greber’s evidence that the net value of the contents may be as low

Child and Spousal Support

Background

[
120
]

There
are a number of issues involved in determining the appropriate support
arrangements between the parties, including each party’s income and means,
child support, s. 7 expenses, spousal support and retroactive adjustments. I
deal with each of these below.

Dr. Weisleder’s Income and Means for Support Purposes

Income

[
121
]

Dr.
Weisleder is an orthopedic surgeon. He earns OHIP income, including through
performing surgery. Orthopedic surgery is physically taxing work.

[
122
]

Dr.
Weisleder also earns non-OHIP income through, among other things, his
medical/legal consulting.

[
123
]

Dr.
Weisleder is presently 58 years old. He currently works very long hours. He
expects that he will soon have to reduce the hours he works. He also expects
that he will have to stop performing surgery at some point in the foreseeable
future. As he ages, his stamina is waning. The long hours and physical nature
of the surgeries he performs are taking a toll on him.

[
124
]

The
parties disagree on how to assess Dr. Weisleder’s income and means.

[
125
]

Since
2016, Dr. Weisleder is no longer depositing his non-OHIP income into 128.
Rather, he has incorporated a new entity, Louis Weisleder Medical Professional
Corporation (“PC”) into which he deposits his OHIP and his non-OHIP income. He
and the children are shareholders of PC.

[
126
]

Up
until the end of 2017, Dr. Weisleder was able to dividend out income to the
children from PC to be offset against their tuition credits. This resulted in
them obtaining the benefit of his income nearly tax-free. However, the parties
agree that changes to the tax laws will prevent Dr. Weisleder from doing so in
the future.  Rather, distributions to the children from the corporation will be
taxed at the highest marginal rate.

[
127
]

Because
of this tax structure, Dr. Weisleder was able, up to 2017, to make his income
available for the family needs on a more tax effective basis than if he had
paid personal income tax at his marginal rate on the totality of his income.

[
128
]

Dr.
Weisleder engaged an expert, Alla Levit, to give evidence as to his income in
2016 and his projected income in 2017. Ms. Levit was qualified as an expert at
trial. Ms. Bedzow did not dispute her qualifications.

[
129
]

Ms.
Levit explained that in order to calculate Dr. Weisleder’s income for support
purposes for 2016 and 2017, she had to account for the tax efficient manner in
which Dr. Weisleder had been able to access his income for family needs. To do
so, she needed to gross up the amounts dividended out to the children to
reflect what he would have had to earn were he paying tax at his marginal tax
rate on the entirety of the income and still had the same amount of net income.

[
130
]

Based
on Ms. Levit’s calculations, Dr. Weisleder’s income for support purposes for
2016 was $867,000. Ms. Bedzow accepts this calculation.

[
131
]

Ms.
Levit’s calculation of Dr. Weisleder’s 2017 income was based on ten months of
actual data and two months of projected data. This was necessary to prepare the
report in adequate time for trial. Ms. Levit’s calculation of Dr. Weisleder’s
2017 income for support purposes (that is, after gross-up) was $794,000.

[
132
]

Ms.
Bedzow disputes the 2017 income calculation. She argues that Dr. Weisleder’s
2017 income is not substantially different than his 2016 income because his
gross billings were not substantially different. At trial, Ms. Levit testified
that she considered her projection having regard to the actual 2017 data which
Dr. Weisleder provided to her in 2018 (for the months for which she had
projected billings) and concluded that her projections of Dr. Weisleder’s gross
income were accurate to within 1%.

[
133
]

I
accept Ms. Levit’s evidence. Her methodology was fair and took into account
matters like personal expenses that were run through the corporation. I thus
find that Dr. Weisleder’s income for support purposes in 2017 was $794,000.

[
134
]

Ms.
Levit also testified as to the effect of the tax changes on Dr. Weisleder’s
income going forward. She adjusted Dr. Weisleder’s 2016 and 2017 gross income
on the basis that he would no longer have the same tax advantage with respect
to dividends to the children. In the result, Dr. Weisleder’s income would have
been $729,000 for 2016 and $652,000 for 2017. I accept that these figures
provide the income that Dr. Weisleder would have earned in 2016 and 2017 had
the tax structure that will be in place in 2018 been in place then.

[
135
]

Ms.
Bedzow argues that Dr. Weisleder’s income going forward should be assessed at
$750,000, a figure which she may have reached on the assumption that Dr.
Weisleder could use 128 to distribute income to the children. In my view, this
figure does not adequately account for the tax advantages that Dr. Weisleder
will lose beginning in 2018.

[
136
]

I
conclude that it is reasonable to calculate Dr. Weisleder’s income for support
purposes based on the latest available income information, adjusted to account
for the tax structure that will be in place in 2018. I thus assume that Dr.
Weisleder’s 2018 income for support purposes is $652,000.

Dr. Weisleder’ Means

[
137
]

In
addition to Dr. Weisleder’s income, there is the question of the other means
available to him.

[
138
]

Dr.
Weisleder owns real property with about $900,000 in equity, and has savings of
about $500,000. He is also burdened by significant debt. His financial
statement from December 2017 demonstrates that, as of the date he swore it, his
assets outweigh his debts by about $100,000.

[
139
]

The
dispute between the parties over Dr. Weisleder’s means relates to 128 and the
trust. Ms. Bedzow argues that Dr. Weisleder is the alter ego of 128 and the
trust such that their assets are available for the use of the family. Ms.
Bedzow argues that this is an appropriate case in which to pierce the corporate
veil.

[
140
]

A
contextual approach is required when one considers whether to pierce the
corporate veil. A court will not enforce the “separate entities” principle when
it would yield a result too flagrantly opposed to justice:
Debora v. Debora
(2006)
,

83 O.R. (3d) 181 (C.A.), at para. 24 [“
Debora
”]
.

[
141
]

In
general, the court will pierce the corporate veil in family law cases when
three circumstances are present: (i) the individual is in complete control of
finances, policy, and business practices of the company; (ii) the control must
have been used by the individual to commit fraud or a wrong that would unjustly
deprive a claimant of her rights; and (iii) the misconduct must be the reason
for the third party’s injury or loss:
Wildman v. Wildman
(2006)
,
2006 CanLII 33540 (ON CA)
, 82
O.R. (3d) 401 (C.A.), at para.
31
[“
Wildman”
].

[
142
]

In
order to pierce the corporate veil, it is not necessary that a company have
been created with an improper purpose in mind; rather it is sufficient if the corporation
is used for an improper purpose:
Wildman
,
at para.
38
.

[
143
]

An
important consideration is whether the interests of third parties will be
affected:
Debora,
at para. 25.

[
144
]

Unlike
the cases provided to me in which the corporate veil was pierced, in this case,
Dr. Weisleder has no economic interest in 128 or the Family Trust. While I
accept that he has solely controlled both 128 and the trust, and while it has
been his income that has been the source of the accumulation of assets in 128
and the trust, from the outset, he did not own it.

[
145
]

I
have already found, in para. 82, that the money he took from 128 was a
bona
fide

(2002)

Spousal Support

Prospective Spousal Support

[
192
]

The
parties agree that Ms. Bedzow is entitled to spousal support. They also agree
on the legal framework within which the determination of quantum must be made.

[
193
]

In
particular, in making an order for spousal support, the court must consider the
condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse, including the
length of time the spouses cohabited, the functions performed by each spouse
during cohabitation and any order, agreement or arrangement relating to support
of either spouse:
Divorce Act
, s. 15.2(4).

[
194
]

The
condition of a spouse includes factors such as their age, health, needs,
obligations, dependence and their station in life. The means of a spouse
includes all financial resources, capital assets, income from employment and
any other sources from which the spouse derives gains or benefits. The needs of
a spouse take into consideration the accustomed lifestyle of the spouse,
subject to the ability to pay:
Thompson v. Thompson
,
2013 ONSC 5500
, at
para.
47
. I have reviewed many of these factors in my analysis with respect to
each party’s income and means, at paras. 121-149 and 150-169.

[
195
]

Section
15.2(6)
of the
Divorce Act
provides that a spousal support order has the
following objectives:

a.

To
recognize any economic advantages or disadvantages to the spouses arising from
the marriage or its breakdown;

b.

To
apportion between the spouses any financial consequences arising from the care
of any child of the marriage over and above any obligation for the support of
any child of the marriage;

c.

To
relieve any economic hardship of the spouses arising from the breakdown of the
marriage;

d.

To
promote the economic self-sufficiency of each spouse within a reasonable period
of time insofar as it is practicable.

[
196
]

All
four objectives must be considered when spousal support is claimed; no single
objective is paramount:
Moge v. Moge,
1992 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 813,

at p. 847.

[
197
]

Considering
the first objective of spousal support, I note that there is no question that
Ms. Bedzow limited her career opportunities to care for the children and
largely took on a traditional role in the marriage. Although I accept that Dr.
Weisleder was always an involved father, Ms. Bedzow’s availability to the
children and for duties around the home allowed Dr. Weisleder the freedom to
focus on his career as and when necessary.

[
198
]

With
respect to the second objective, Ms. Bedzow was, for many years, the primary
caregiver to the children, and as a consequence, limited her career prospects.

[
199
]

With
respect to the third objective of spousal support, Ms. Bedzow has suffered
greater economic hardship arising out of the breakdown of the marriage than has
Dr. Weisleder. Dr. Weisleder continues to reside in the matrimonial home and
lives in much the same way he always has. Ms. Bedzow is in more precarious
financial circumstances. I accept that the separation, together with her cancer
diagnosis and other health problems, created a situation of tremendous stress
from which she has suffered. I accept that it was difficult for her to maintain
even the modest level of income she earned during the marriage. That is not,
however, a situation that should continue in the future given her improved
health and the resolution of this action.

[
200
]

Notwithstanding
the negative effects of the separation on Ms. Bedzow, I also note that she
rents a large apartment, and has continued to travel extensively, although some
of her travels have been paid for by her mother or her new partner. Thus, while
I accept that she has experienced financial challenges, in my view she has
continued to live in comfortable circumstances.

[
201
]

I
also note that the economic hardship in this case does not arise only out of
marriage breakdown, but out of the financial reality that the parties always
lived beyond their means, and relied on debt to maintain their high standard of
living. This has become much more difficult because the parties must now
maintain two households and meet the increased educational expenses of the
children. Both parties must accept a reduction in the standard of living they
enjoyed during marriage. It wasn’t affordable then and it is even less
affordable now.

[
202
]

With
respect to the fourth objective of spousal support, there is no reason that Ms.
Bedzow cannot become more self-sufficient economically. She is positioned to
grow her speech pathology practice. I see no impediment to her doing so,
especially at the level at which I have imputed income to her (that is, roughly
nine hours of client care per week plus associated administrative and research
work). Even still, work at this level will not support a standard of living
that even begins to approach that which the parties enjoyed during marriage.

[
203
]

Based
on the roles the parties assumed during their marriage, the length of their
marriage and Dr. Weisleder’s admission as to entitlement, I find that Ms.
Bedzow is entitled to compensatory support. In my view, she is also entitled to
non-compensatory support in view of the financial challenges she has faced
since separation, while Dr. Weisleder has continued to live in the same manner
as he did prior to separation.

[
204
]

The
parties agree that the order I make should be indefinite without a built-in
review. Rather, the order would be reviewable on a material change.

[
205
]

In
terms of quantum, Ms. Bedzow argues that spousal support should equalize the
parties’ net disposable income. Dr. Weisleder argues that the
Spousal
Support Advisory Guidelines
(Carol Rogerson and Rollie Thompson, 2008) [“SSAG”]
address the consequences arising from marriage or its breakdown, but do not
speak to equalizing income:
Celotti v. Celotti,
2007 CarswellOnt 4137
(S.C.J.), at para. 56
. Rather, he states that the SSAG calculations are
appropriate, notwithstanding the fact that the guidelines themselves warn that
their use might not be appropriate at Dr. Weisleder’s level of income.

[
206
]

In
my view, prospective spousal support should be calculated on the basis that Dr.
Weisleder’s income is $652,000 per year and Ms. Bedzow’s income is $50,000 per
year, net of business expenses but gross of taxes. The calculation should

based on the roles the parties adopted during the marriage, the fact that Ms.

the fact that Ms. Bedzow has experienced greater economic hardship arising from
the breakdown of the marriage, and in recognition of the fact that Dr.
